title: SAM Audio: Segment Anything in Audio
claim: One unified model accepts any combination of visual, temporal-span, and text prompts to separate a target source from a mixture.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, three parallel prompt branches merging into one transformer
description: A single wide left-to-right diagram. On the left, an input box shows a video frame of a woman playing with a dog and its audio waveform, labeled as the audio mixture. Three parallel branches fan out. The top branch, the visual prompt, runs from the video through SAM 2 to a masked dog and then a visual encoder. The middle branch, the span prompt, runs through span selection to a highlighted waveform and then a span encoder. The bottom branch, the text prompt, runs from a text description box holding the query 'dog barking' to a text encoder. The raw mixture also goes through an audio encoder. All encoder outputs, drawn as teal trapezoids, feed a tall blue Diffusion Transformer bar. Its output goes to a teal Decoder, which produces target audio and residual audio waveforms on the right. The colors are teal, purple, and blue on a white background.
caption: Overview of SAM Audio. Given an audio mixture, SAM Audio separates it into target and residual stems, conditioned on any combination of text descriptions (text prompts), visual masks (visual prompts), and temporal intervals (span prompts).
abstract: General audio source separation is a key capability for multimodal AI systems that can perceive and reason about sound. Despite substantial progress in recent years, existing separation models are either domain-specific, designed for fixed categories such as speech or music, or limited in controllability, supporting only a single prompting modality such as text. In this work, we present SAM Audio, a foundation model for general audio separation that unifies text, visual, and temporal span prompting within a single framework. Built on a diffusion transformer architecture, SAM Audio is trained with flow matching on large-scale audio data spanning speech, music, and general sounds, and can flexibly separate target sources described by language, visual masks, or temporal spans. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance across a diverse suite of benchmarks, including general sound, speech, music, and musical instrument separation in both in-the-wild and professionally produced audios, substantially outperforming prior general-purpose and specialized systems. Furthermore, we introduce a new real-world separation benchmark with human-labeled multimodal prompts and a reference-free evaluation model that correlates strongly with human judgment.
